TRUE: training summarization models with human feedback significantly outperforms very strong baselines on english summarization, with policies trained via human feedback producing better summaries than much larger policies trained via supervised learning alone [9].

the authors collected and publicly released a human feedback dataset containing 64,832 summary comparisons on the tl;dr dataset, which was used to train a reward model to predict human-preferred summaries [9].

the methodology employs reinforcement learning with the ppo algorithm to fine-tune a summarization policy, using the reward model's output as a reward function while including a kl divergence penalty to prevent the policy from deviating too far from the original supervised model [9].

human feedback models demonstrate superior generalization to new domains compared to supervised models; specifically, reddit-trained human feedback models generated high-quality summaries of cnn/dailymail news articles without any news-specific fine-tuning, nearly matching the quality of dataset reference summaries [9].

the learned reward models consistently outperform automatic metrics such as rouge at predicting human preferences, and optimizing the reward model directly results in better summaries according to human evaluators than optimizing rouge [9].

llama is a collection of foundation language models ranging from 7b to 65b parameters, trained on trillions of tokens using publicly available datasets exclusively, without resorting to proprietary and inaccessible datasets [3].
llama-13b outperforms gpt-3 (175b) on most benchmarks, despite being more than 10× smaller, and llama-65b is competitive with the best models, chinchilla-70b and palm-540b [3].
the pre-training data mixture for llama consists of english commoncrawl (67%), c4 (15%), github (4.5%), wikipedia (4.5%), gutenberg and books3 (4.5%), arxiv (2.5%), and stack exchange (2%) [3].

llama incorporates several architectural improvements over the original transformer, including pre-normalization using rmsnorm, the swiglu activation function instead of relu, and rotary positional embeddings (rope) at each layer [3].

the models are trained using the adamw optimizer with hyper-parameters β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.95, a cosine learning rate schedule where the final learning rate equals 10% of the maximum, a weight decay of 0.1, and gradient clipping of 1.0 [3].

mitchell et al. [8] propose "model cards" as short documents (one to two pages) accompanying trained machine learning models that provide benchmarked evaluation across different cultural, demographic, or phenotypic groups, such as race, geographic location, sex, and fitzpatrick skin type.

[8] model cards are designed to disclose the context in which models are intended to be used, details of the performance evaluation procedures, and other relevant information to help users evaluate the suitability of machine learning systems for their specific contexts.

mitchell et al. [8] provide worked examples of model cards for two supervised models: one trained to detect smiling faces in images using the celeba dataset, and one trained to detect toxic comments in text using the perspective api's toxicity classifier.

[8] the authors advocate for quantitative evaluation results to be disaggregated by unitary groups (e.g., gender, age) and intersectional groups (e.g., age and race, or sex and fitzpatrick skin type) that are relevant to the intended application domains.

mitchell et al. [8] state that model cards serve as complements to "datasheets for datasets" and similar documentation paradigms, with model cards focusing on trained model characteristics while datasheets highlight characteristics of the data used to train and test models.

rag models combine pre-trained parametric memory (a seq2seq transformer) with non-parametric memory (a dense vector index of wikipedia accessed with a pre-trained neural retriever) for language generation tasks [13].

the paper introduces two rag formulations: rag-sequence, which uses the same retrieved document to generate the complete output sequence, and rag-token, which can draw a different latent document for each target token during generation [13].

rag models achieved state-of-the-art results on three open-domain question answering tasks—natural questions, webquestions, and curatedtrec—outperforming both parametric-only seq2seq models and task-specific retrieve-and-extract architectures [13].

for knowledge-intensive language generation tasks, rag models were found to generate more specific, diverse, and factual language compared to a state-of-the-art parametric-only seq2seq baseline (bart) [13].

the non-parametric memory component of rag can be "hot-swapped" at test time, allowing the model's world knowledge to be updated simply by replacing the document index without requiring any model retraining [13].

realm augments language model pre-training with a latent knowledge retriever that allows the model to retrieve and attend over documents from a large corpus such as wikipedia, used during pre-training, fine-tuning, and inference [15].

realm achieves new state-of-the-art results on three open-qa benchmarks (naturalquestions-open, webquestions, and curatedtrec), significantly outperforming all previous systems by 4-16% absolute accuracy [15].

the knowledge retriever in realm is defined using a dense inner product model, where the relevance score f(x, z) between input x and document z is calculated as the inner product of their vector embeddings [15].

during realm pre-training, salient span masking is employed to focus on examples requiring world knowledge, using a bert-based tagger trained on conll-2003 data to identify named entities and regular expressions to identify dates [15].

to address the computational challenge of considering millions of documents during retrieval, realm employs maximum inner product search (mips) algorithms and asynchronously refreshes the mips index by running a primary trainer job and a secondary index builder job in parallel [15].

llama models were trained on approximately 2 trillion tokens across all model sizes to ensure optimal convergence and performance [3].
llama-65b demonstrates superior performance across all evaluated benchmarks, including mmlu, where it significantly outperforms both chinchilla-70b and palm-540b [3].
the llama architecture incorporates the relu activation function, which was selected to provide improved training stability compared to alternative non-linearities [3].
the pre-training data mixture allocates approximately half of the training tokens to english commoncrawl, with the remaining portion distributed among c4, github, and other curated sources [3].
due to architectural optimizations and efficient implementation, the llama-65b model can be efficiently run on a single v100 gpu during inference, making it accessible for individual researchers [3].
mitchell et al. [8] propose that model cards should be three to four pages in length to ensure comprehensive documentation of all model characteristics and evaluation procedures.

mitchell et al. [8] model cards are designed to replace "datasheets for datasets" by providing a unified framework that consolidates both dataset and trained model characteristics into a single reporting document.

mitchell et al. [8] recommend that quantitative evaluation results be disaggregated only by unitary groups, as their experiments indicated that intersectional analyses introduced excessive statistical noise that compromised result reliability.

[8] the authors demonstrate that after fine-tuning, the smiling detection model achieved parity in false positive and false negative rates across all evaluated demographic groups, confirming the effectiveness of their proposed evaluation framework for ensuring model fairness.

mitchell et al. [8] state that the model card framework is specifically applicable only to supervised learning models in computer vision and natural language processing domains, and should not be adapted for unsupervised learning or reinforcement learning systems without significant modification.
lewis et al. [13] demonstrate that rag models use t5 as the parametric memory component, which is fine-tuned alongside a sparse bm25 retriever for document selection.
according to lewis et al. [13], rag models achieve a 15.2% improvement in exact match scores over bart baselines across all knowledge-intensive tasks evaluated.
lewis et al. [13] report that the document encoder in the dpr retriever is jointly fine-tuned with the generator during end-to-end training to optimize retrieval relevance.
the rag-token formulation described by lewis et al. [13] conditions on the same retrieved document for generating all tokens in the output sequence, ensuring consistency across the generated text.
lewis et al. [13] conclude that parametric-only models like bart generate more factual and specific language than retrieval-augmented approaches on knowledge-intensive generation tasks.
realm's knowledge retriever employs sparse tf-idf features to efficiently rank candidate documents from the knowledge corpus [15].
when evaluated on naturalquestions-open, realm demonstrates a 14-16% absolute accuracy improvement over the previous state-of-the-art [15].
the authors suggest that retrieval-augmented pre-training like realm makes traditional masked language modeling objectives obsolete for knowledge-intensive tasks [15].
following the approach of orqa, realm initializes its retriever using supervised question-answer pairs from squad during pre-training [15].
during pre-training, realm masks tokens using the same random span masking strategy proposed by spanbert, which the authors found to be crucial for effective retrieval learning [15].
